docs.title: PinGoblin UPS HAT+
docs.text:
The UPS HAT+ keeps a Raspberry Pi running from a 2-cell lithium-ion battery when mains power fails, and shuts the Pi down cleanly before the battery runs flat. This site is the documentation for the board and its software.

  • UPS HAT+ User Manual

    Setting up and using the board and the UPS Pack: specifications, safety, battery requirements, installation, operation, troubleshooting and electrical characteristics.

  • UPS HAT+ API

    The ups_hat Python and MicroPython library: installation, concepts, power-off integration, fault codes and the full API reference.

docs.title: PinGoblin UPS HAT+ Library
docs.text:
The ups_hat library provides access to everything the PinGoblin UPS HAT+ can measure, control or report. This code will run on CPython / Micropython compatible boards such as the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and ESP32 and needs no third-party packages.

The library talks to the below IC's on the USB HAT's I²C bus.

Chip Function Address BQ25798 (U2) Charger, power path, ADC, ship mode 0x6B STUSB4500 (U1) USB-C PD sink controller 0x28

Components such as connected battery packs and the HAT's 5.1 V converter (TPS54620 buck) do not have an I²C interface. This library works out their state from indirect measurements. Where an indirect measurement has been made, and results in a fault conditionl, the fault will be reported as inferred. Rev D has no battery temperature sensor: R4/R5 hold the charger's TS input at 60 % of REGN (normal temperature), and the library reports BOARD_TS_FAULT if that reading leaves 50–70 %. All PinGolbin battery packs contain temperature sensing, high-temperature charging cut-offs, over/under charge cut-offs and cell balancing.

USB-C adapter

The adapter must offer USB PD at 9 V or 15 V, 3 A. A 5 V-only adapter will run a lightly loaded Pi but is not supported (the library will report PD_LOW_CONTRACT or PD_NO_CONTRACT).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from ups_hat import UPS

ups = UPS(cells_parallel=1, cell_capacity_mah=3000)   # Raspberry Pi
s = ups.poll()
print(s.vbat, s.ibat, s.soc, s.on_battery)
print(s.fault_codes())
print(ups.report(s))

To receive events:

@ups.on_fault
def alert(fault):
    print(fault)            # [WARNING] BAT_HIGH_RESISTANCE: Battery path resistance is high. (ohm=0.41)

ups.run(interval_s=2)       # poll forever

docs.title: Fault codes
docs.text:
These fault codes are listed in CATALOGUE and have the following attributes:

  • Severity: info needs no action, warning needs attention, critical needs action now.
  • Source: charger and pd faults are read from the chips; bus means a chip did not answer; pi comes from the Raspberry Pi 5 firmware; inferred faults are calculated indirectly from measurements over time. Most inferred faults are strong hints rather than proof of a fault, and must persist for a few seconds to a few minutes before they are reported.
Code Severity Source Meaning What to do BUS_CHARGER_MISSING critical bus Charger (BQ25798, 0x6B) is not answering on I2C. Check that I2C is enabled and the HAT is seated. If it persists the charger may be damaged. BUS_PD_MISSING warning bus USB-C controller (STUSB4500, 0x28) is not answering on I2C. Power is unaffected but PD information is unavailable. Re-seat the HAT. CHG_CONVERTER_OCP critical charger Charger converter over-current. Possible board fault or short on SYS. CHG_IBAT_OCP critical charger Battery over-current. Check for a short or a damaged cell; check battery wiring. CHG_IBAT_REGULATION info charger Battery discharge current is being limited. — CHG_IBUS_OCP warning charger Input over-current. The load is above what the adapter can supply. CHG_INPUT_LIMITED info charger Adapter is at its current or voltage limit. Use a USB-C PD adapter that offers 9 V or 15 V at 3 A (15 V for full load while charging). CHG_POOR_SOURCE warning charger Weak adapter detected. Use a USB-C PD adapter that offers 9 V or 15 V at 3 A, and a good cable. CHG_PRECHARGE_TIMER_EXPIRED warning charger Pre-charge timer expired: the battery did not recover from deep discharge. A cell is probably damaged. Replace both cells. CHG_RESET_DETECTED warning charger Charger settings had returned to defaults (power-on reset). The charger lost power: pack disconnected, pack protection tripped or SYS brown-out. Settings re-applied. CHG_THERMAL_REGULATION info charger Charger is reducing current to limit its temperature. Improve airflow. CHG_THERMAL_SHUTDOWN critical charger Charger thermal shutdown. Improve airflow; reduce load or charge current. CHG_TIMER_EXPIRED warning charger Fast-charge safety timer expired before the battery was full. The cells may be worn, or the charge current is too low for their capacity (check cells_parallel). CHG_TRICKLE_TIMER_EXPIRED warning charger Trickle-charge timer expired: the battery voltage stayed very low. Check the pack cable; a cell may be dead or the pack fuse blown. CHG_VAC_OVP critical charger Input (VAC) over-voltage. Unplug the adapter; it is faulty or not USB-C PD compliant. CHG_VBAT_OVP critical charger Battery over-voltage. Check the cells are Li-ion 3.6/3.7 V types wired as 2S. Charging is stopped. CHG_VBUS_OVP critical charger USB-C input over-voltage. Unplug the adapter; it is faulty or not USB-C PD compliant. CHG_VSYS_OVP critical charger System rail (SYS) over-voltage. Board fault; disconnect power. CHG_VSYS_SHORT critical charger System rail (SYS) short circuit. Remove the Pi and accessories; if it persists the board is faulty. CHG_WATCHDOG_EXPIRED warning charger Charger I2C watchdog expired; charger settings returned to defaults. The library re-applies its settings automatically. PD_CAPABILITY_MISMATCH warning pd Adapter cannot supply the current requested. Use a PD adapter that offers 9 V or 15 V at 3 A. PD_CC_OVERVOLTAGE critical pd Over-voltage on the USB-C CC lines. Unplug the cable; it or the adapter is faulty. PD_CONFIG_MISMATCH warning pd USB-C controller PDO settings differ from the factory settings. Run UPS.restore_pd_defaults() or contact support. PD_LOW_CONTRACT info pd Adapter offered less than 9 V. Use a PD adapter that offers 9 V or 15 V at 3 A. PD_NO_CONTRACT info pd Adapter is not USB PD (5 V only). Not supported: the Pi gets about 11 W at most and charging is slow. Use a USB-C PD adapter that offers 9 V or 15 V at 3 A. ADAPTER_INSUFFICIENT warning inferred Running partly from battery while the adapter is connected. The adapter cannot carry the load. Use a USB-C PD adapter that offers 15 V at 3 A. BAT_ABSENT critical inferred No battery detected. Plug the pack's XT30 lead into J3, switch the pack ON and check its cells are fitted. A pack that is switched off, has tripped its protection or temperature cut-off, or has a blown fuse also reads as absent. BAT_CAPACITY_LOW warning inferred Measured battery capacity is well below the rated capacity. The cells are worn, or cell_capacity_mah is set too high. BAT_CHARGE_BLOCKED warning inferred Charging has stopped before the battery is full. The pack's protection (HY2120) has blocked charging: one cell reached 4.25 V, so the cells are out of balance. Check the cells in the pack. BAT_CRITICAL critical inferred Battery critically low; shut down now. Connect the adapter. BAT_DEEPLY_DISCHARGED warning inferred Battery is below 6.0 V (deeply discharged). Leave on the adapter; if it does not recover within an hour replace both cells. BAT_EARLY_CUTOFF warning inferred Power was lost on battery while the pack still had charge. One cell may be weak, or the load exceeded the pack's protection limit. Check the cells. BAT_HIGH_RESISTANCE warning inferred Battery path resistance is high. Clean the pack's cell contacts and check the pack cable and connectors. A gradual rise means the cells are ageing. BAT_IMBALANCE_SUSPECTED warning inferred Cells appear to be out of balance. Charging repeatedly stops early. Balancing will correct small differences over several charges; replace both cells with a matched pair if it persists. BAT_LOW warning inferred Battery low. Connect the adapter. BAT_PARALLEL_CELL_MISSING warning inferred Configured for 2S2P but the battery behaves like 2S1P. Check that all four cells are fitted, or set cells_parallel=1. BAT_SELF_DISCHARGE warning inferred Battery needs recharging unusually often while on the adapter. A cell may be leaking charge. Replace both cells if it persists. BAT_WIRING_FAULT critical inferred Battery reads like a single cell or a reversed cell. Check both cells in the pack are fitted the right way round. Charging is stopped. BOARD_HOT warning inferred Charger temperature is high. Improve airflow around the HAT. BOARD_OVERHEAT critical inferred Charger temperature is very high. Shut down and improve cooling. BOARD_TS_FAULT warning inferred Charger TS input is out of range; charging is blocked. R4/R5 (TS divider, 60 % of REGN) are damaged or missing. Return the board for repair. CABLE_RESISTANCE_HIGH warning inferred High voltage drop in the USB-C cable or connector. Use a shorter or better USB-C cable (rated 3 A or 5 A). OUTPUT_5V_FAULT critical inferred 5 V output is low while the battery/adapter rail is healthy. The 5.1 V stage is current limiting or faulty, or the Pi is drawing more than 5 A. OUTPUT_OVERLOAD warning inferred Output power is near the 25 W limit. Reduce the load on the Pi and its USB ports. PI_EXTERNAL_SUPPLY info inferred The Pi appears to be powered from its own USB-C supply. The UPS is not carrying the load. Remove the Pi's own supply to get battery backup. PI_UNDERVOLTAGE warning pi The Pi reports under-voltage on its 5 V input. Reduce load; if SYS is healthy the 5.1 V stage is current limiting. PI_UNDERVOLTAGE_OCCURRED info pi The Pi has seen under-voltage since boot. —

docs.title: Polling
docs.text:
Call poll() every 1–5 s. Each call:

  • reads the charger ADC, status, faults and latched flags, plus the USB-C status and contract;
  • updates the battery model;
  • re-applies the charger settings if the charger has reset;
  • evaluates every fault rule and returns a Snapshot.

This library reads the chargers latched flag registers on every poll. Faults that appear briefly but are cleared between polls will be captured and reported once, with transient=True.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Volts, amps, watts, °C, mAh, percent and hours. For battery current, a positive value means charging and a negative value means discharging.

docs.title: State of charge
docs.text:
• SoC is calculated from the battery current.
  • It is set to 100 % when the charger reports charge done.
  • It is corrected from the resting voltage after 30 minutes with no load.
  • 100 % means full at the configured charge voltage (8.20 V by default), so capacities are usable capacities.
  • Capacity is learned automatically after a deep discharge from full.
  • Similarly, battery-path resistance is learned from load steps.
  • A state_file keeps what has been learned between runs.

docs.title: Fault sources
docs.text: Source Meaning charger Read from the BQ25798. pd Read from the STUSB4500. bus A chip did not answer. pi Read from the Raspberry Pi 5 firmware with vcgencmd. inferred Worked out from measurements over time. A strong hint rather than proof; most must persist for a few seconds to a few minutes before they are reported.

docs.title: Settings the library enforces
docs.text:
With auto_configure=True:

  • charger I²C watchdog off, so the settings hold;
  • charge voltage and charge current as configured;
  • ADC on at 15 bits;
  • discharge-current sensing on, so the battery current is valid on battery power;
  • SFET_PRESENT set, which unlocks ship mode and the SW1 wake-up.

The library checks these every minute and re-applies them after a charger reset. When it does, it reports CHG_RESET_DETECTED. On every change of USB-C contract, it sets the charger input current limit from the contract.

docs.title: Hardware cut-off
docs.text: If no software acts, the HAT's 5.1 V output switches off when the pack falls to about 5.6 V (2.8 V per cell) and back on above about 6.1 V. If running, the library's own shutdown will occur earlier as it is set to 5 % SoC or 6.2 V under load, whichever comes first.

docs.title: Low-level drivers
docs.text:
Use the drivers directly when you need register access:

from ups_hat import BQ25798, STUSB4500, LinuxI2C

i2c = LinuxI2C(1)
chg = BQ25798(i2c)
print(chg.read_adc())                 # ADCReading(vbus=..., ibus=..., vbat=...)
print(chg.status()["charge_state_text"], chg.faults(), chg.read_flags())
chg.charge_current = 1.0
print(hex(chg.dump()[0x1C]))

pd = STUSB4500(i2c)
print(pd.status(), pd.contract, pd.sink_pdos())

The BQ25798 driver deliberately offers no way to turn on OTG, ACFET/RBFET or MPPT: OTG would drive voltage back into the USB-C port, which is sink-only. The STUSB4500 NVM has limited write endurance, so it is programmed once in the factory test jig and writing it needs confirm=True.

docs.title: Python (e.g. Pi)
docs.text:
1. Enable I²C: `sudo raspi-config` → Interface Options → I2C. Alternatively, add `dtparam=i2c_arm=on` to `/boot/firmware/config.txt`.
2. Install the library straight from GitHub:

    ```sh
    sudo pip install git+https://github.com/PinGoblin/UPS_HAT   # add --break-system-packages on Bookworm
    ups-hat status                                              # or: python3 -m ups_hat.cli status
    ```

    To install a particular release, add its tag: `git+https://github.com/PinGoblin/UPS_HAT@v1.4.0`. From a downloaded copy of the repository, use `sudo pip install .` instead.

The library opens `/dev/i2c-1` by itself. Run it as root, or add your user to the `i2c` group.

docs.title: MicroPython (e.g. ESP32)
docs.text:
Copy the ups_hat folder to the board:

```sh
mpremote cp -r ups_hat :
```

The board then loads the files without compiling them, which needs much less RAM. `README.txt` in the zip shows the `.mpy` version the files were built for; it must match your firmware.

**Source files with `mip`.** Installs the `.py` files from GitHub into `/lib` on the board:

```sh
mpremote mip install github:PinGoblin/UPS_HAT/micropython            # latest
mpremote mip install github:PinGoblin/UPS_HAT/micropython@v1.4.0     # a release
```

The board compiles these when you import them, which needs extra RAM: see [MicroPython notes](micropython.md) for how much.

Then, for example on a Raspberry Pi Pico:

```python
from machine import I2C, Pin
from ups_hat import UPS

ups = UPS(I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), scl=Pin(5), freq=400000), pi_monitor=False)
print(ups.report())
```

docs.title: Command-line tool
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi only.

Command What it does ups-hat status One-off report (the default). ups-hat watch [secs] Live report, refreshed every secs seconds (default 2). ups-hat json One snapshot as JSON. ups-hat faults List every fault code. ups-hat registers Dump the charger registers. ups-hat pd USB-C PD configuration and contract. ups-hat poweroff [low] systemd-shutdown hook: ship mode, reset or nothing.

The tool reads UPS_HAT_CELLS_PARALLEL (default 1), UPS_HAT_CELL_MAH (default 3000) and UPS_HAT_STATE (default /var/lib/ups-hat/state.json) from the environment.

docs.title: RAM use
docs.text:
Measured in CI on MicroPython v1.25.0 (unix port), importing the library, creating a UPS on the register simulator and polling it twice. The 32-bit build is the closest match to RP2040, RP2350 and ESP32 boards.

Build Files RAM in use after import RAM in use while running Smallest heap that works 32-bit .mpy (recommended) 68 KB 72 KB 90 KB 32-bit .py (compiled on the board) 72 KB 77 KB 130 KB 64-bit .mpy 101 KB 109 KB 142 KB 64-bit .py 107 KB 114 KB 195 KB
  • "Smallest heap that works" is the figure to compare with your board: run import gc; gc.collect(); print(gc.mem_free()) before importing anything. It includes the extra memory the compiler needs while it reads .py files, which is why .py needs about 40 KB more than .mpy.
  • .mpy files are recommended. They skip on-board compilation and leave the most RAM for your own code. Get them from the latest release; see Installation.
  • To save more RAM, freeze the package into the firmware. The library's code then runs from flash and only its working data uses the heap.
  • The figures are measured on the unix port, not on a board. Real boards also need RAM for your own program and for drivers such as Wi-Fi. CI re-measures on every pull request: see the micropython job's summary.

docs.title: Other notes
docs.text:
• Docstrings are discarded when MicroPython compiles the code, so they cost no RAM. They do take flash space in the .py files; .mpy files leave them out.
  • The command-line tool and Pi 5 monitoring are not available on MicroPython. Pass pi_monitor=False.
  • state_file works on boards with a filesystem, but flash wears with frequent writes. The library saves at most every 5 minutes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
examples/micropython_main.py:

import time
from machine import I2C, Pin
from ups_hat import UPS, CRITICAL

i2c = I2C(0, sda=Pin(4), scl=Pin(5), freq=400000)
ups = UPS(i2c, cells_parallel=1, cell_capacity_mah=3000, pi_monitor=False)

while True:
    s = ups.poll()
    print(s.vbat, s.ibat, s.soc, s.fault_codes())
    time.sleep(2)

docs.title: Power-off integration on linux boards (e.g. Raspberry Pi)
docs.text:
1. Install the library.
  2. Copy examples/ to /usr/local/lib/ups-hat/examples/.
  3. Install the service and the shutdown hook, then start the service:
sudo cp examples/systemd/ups-hat.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo cp examples/systemd/ups-hat-shutdown /usr/lib/systemd/system-shutdown/
sudo chmod +x /usr/lib/systemd/system-shutdown/ups-hat-shutdown
sudo systemctl enable --now ups-hat

Edit the Environment= lines in ups-hat.service to match your cells.

docs.title: The daemon
docs.text:
examples/pi_daemon.py:

  • polls every 2 s and logs faults to the journal (journalctl -u ups-hat);
  • writes /run/ups-hat/status.json;
  • at low battery, creates /run/ups-lowbatt and runs systemctl poweroff.

docs.title: The shutdown hook
docs.text:
The hook runs as the very last step of a power-off or halt. It never acts on a reboot. It calls power_off(), which does one of three things:

Situation Action No adapter Ship mode. The board goes dark. Press SW1 or plug in an adapter to start again. Adapter connected, low-battery shutdown System reset, so the Pi boots on mains instead of sitting halted. Adapter connected, user shutdown Nothing. The Pi halts and the board stays on.

docs.title: Safety and limits
docs.text:
• The charge voltage is clamped to 7.0–8.4 V, the charge current to 3.0 A and the input current limit to 3.0 A.
  • The USB-C adapter must offer USB PD at 9 V or 15 V, 3 A. With 9 V the adapter covers about 22 W of Pi load; above that, and with any 5 V source, the pack makes up the difference.
  • power_off(), ship_mode(), shutdown_mode() and system_reset() need the SDRV ship FET. On a board built without it, pass ship_fet=False; these calls then raise NotSupported.
  • BAT_WIRING_FAULT stops charging while the pack reads like a single or reversed cell (2.5–4.6 V). Charging resumes when the reading is normal again.
  • Inferred battery faults are estimates. Confirm them by measuring the cells before replacing anything.

docs.title: Testing without hardware
docs.text: tests/sim.py simulates both chips at register level. Run the full suite with python -m pytest, with no extra packages using python -m unittest discover -s tests, or run the end-to-end scenarios on MicroPython with micropython tests/scenarios.py. See Testing.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: The library is tested without hardware. tests/sim.py simulates the BQ25798 charger and the STUSB4500 USB-C controller at register level, and the tests drive those simulators.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
pytest (recommended)Standard library onlyMicroPython 
pip install -r requirements-test.txt     # pytest, coverage, hypothesis
python -m pytest

With branch coverage:

python -m coverage run -m pytest
python -m coverage report                # fails below 95 %
python -m coverage html                  # htmlcov/index.html

No packages needed; runs on CPython 3.8 or later:

python -m unittest discover -s tests

The property tests then run with a seeded random sampler instead of Hypothesis.

The end-to-end scenarios run unchanged under MicroPython:

micropython tests/scenarios.py

Warnings are errors under pytest (filterwarnings = error in pyproject.toml), so an unclosed file or a deprecated call fails the run.

docs.title: What is tested
docs.text:
File Covers test_compat.py The CPython/MicroPython layer: signed values, clamping, clocks, and the MicroPython code paths. test_bus.py I2CDevice register and bit-field helpers, error wrapping, LinuxI2C (with /dev/i2c-N mocked) and open_bus. test_faults.py Every catalogue entry is well formed, has advice when needed, and is raised by board.py; Fault formatting; the fault codes page is up to date. test_battery.py The OCV table, coulomb counting, rest correction, capacity learning, resistance tracking and the state file round trip. test_bq25798.py Every charger setting: round trip, step rounding and clamping; every on/off setting changes exactly one bit; status, fault and flag decoding; ADC decoding; ship-FET control. test_stusb4500.py PDO and contract decoding, status and events, sink PDO editing, NVM read, write, time-out and encoding. test_board.py The UPS class: missing and returning chips, configuration and repair after a charger reset, power-off decisions, USB-C PD, every fault rule (raised after its debounce time and cleared again), callbacks, the state file, I²C errors in the middle of a poll, and the report. test_pimon.py Raspberry Pi 5 monitoring with vcgencmd mocked: throttle bits, EXT5V_V, non-Pi systems and time-outs. test_cli.py Every ups-hat command and its environment variables. test_packaging.py One version everywhere; the MicroPython file list; a matching .pyi stub and an API page for every module; no CPython-only imports or syntax in the modules MicroPython installs. test_properties.py Invariants for any input (Hypothesis): register fields, setting ranges, NVM encoding, the battery model's bounds, and a fuzz test that poll() never raises whatever the chips report. test_scenarios.py Runs each end-to-end scenario in scenarios.py as its own test.

Time-based fault rules use a simulated clock (tests/helpers.py), so a rule that needs a condition to hold for two minutes is tested in milliseconds.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
Every pull request runs:

  • the suite on CPython 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13 with coverage and Hypothesis, and on 3.8 with the standard library only;
  • mypy and stubtest on the type stubs;
  • the scenarios under MicroPython, plus the RAM measurements described in MicroPython notes.

The coverage report appears in the job summary, and the HTML report is attached to the run as coverage-html.

docs.title: Battery model
docs.text:
This module exposes battery state: state of charge, capacity and resistance.

  • State of charge is counted from IBAT (coulomb counting).
  • It is set to 100 % when the charger reports charge done, and corrected from the open-circuit voltage after the pack has rested for 30 minutes.
  • 100 % means full at the configured charge voltage (8.20 V by default), so capacity figures are usable capacity.

docs.title: BQ25798 charger
docs.text:
This module provides a low-level driver for the TI BQ25798 buck-boost charger (U2, I²C address 0x6B).

Register map: TI datasheet SLUSDV2. 16-bit registers are most significant byte first. Voltages are in volts, currents in amps and temperatures in °C unless the name ends in _mv, _ma or _raw.

The UPS HAT+ does not use OTG (it would drive VBUS on a sink-only USB-C port), the ACFET/RBFET input switches or MPPT, so this driver deliberately offers no way to turn them on. TS has no NTC on Rev D (fixed 60 % divider); ts_ignore is exposed for completeness and is not used by UPS.

This module provides I²C access and exposes the library's exception classes.

Any object with MicroPython's machine.I2C memory methods can carry the I²C bus:

readfrom_mem(addr, reg, nbytes) -> bytes
writeto_mem(addr, reg, buf)

On a Raspberry Pi (CPython), LinuxI2C talks to /dev/i2c-N directly and needs no extra packages.

machine.I2C-compatible wrapper for Linux /dev/i2c-N.

Uses plain read()/write() on the character device, so it needs no third-party package. The Raspberry Pi header I²C (pins 3 and 5) is bus 1.

Can be used as a context manager, which closes the device on exit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default bus int

I²C bus number.

1

Type Description OSError

from ups_hat import LinuxI2C, BQ25798

with LinuxI2C(1) as i2c:
    print(BQ25798(i2c).read_adc())

docs.title: Faults
docs.text:
Fault codes reported by UPS.

Each fault has a stable string code (safe to log or match on), a severity, the source it came from, a one-line message and advice for the user. The full list is CATALOGUE; the Fault codes page shows it as a table.

Source Meaning charger Read from BQ25798 registers. pd Read from STUSB4500 registers. bus An I²C device did not answer. inferred Worked out from measurements over time: a strong hint, not proof. pi Read from the Raspberry Pi 5 firmware (vcgencmd).

docs.title: STUSB4500 USB-C PD
docs.text:
A low-level driver for the ST STUSB4500 USB-C PD sink controller (U1, I²C address 0x28).

The register map and NVM sequence follow ST's public register map and reference software (github.com/usb-c/STUSB4500) and SparkFun's STUSB4500 library.

The negotiated contract (RDO) gives the source PDO position and the current. The source's list of voltages is only on the bus for about 3 ms during negotiation, so the contract voltage is best taken from the charger's VBUS ADC.

docs.title: UPS HAT+ User Manual
docs.text:
The UPS HAT+ keeps a Raspberry Pi running from a 2-cell (2S) lithium-ion battery when mains power fails, and shuts the Pi down cleanly before the battery runs flat. It powers the Pi through the 40-pin header at 5.1 V and up to 5 A, so a Raspberry Pi 5 can run at full load with USB peripherals attached.

This manual covers the UPS HAT+ hardware revision D and its battery, the UPS Pack board Rev B (DUAL or QUAD). Read the safety section before connecting a battery.

UPS HAT+ Rev D (board marking Ver 1.4). The USB-C input is on the left edge, the 40-pin header's pins come through along the top edge, and the yellow XT30 battery connector J3 is at the bottom edge. Rendered from the production Gerber files.

docs.title: Battery requirements
docs.text:
The battery is the UPS Pack board with your own cells, or a ready-made 2S pack that has its own protection. The HAT itself has no cell protection. The cells must meet every item below.

  • Cell type: 18650 lithium-ion (3.6–3.7 V nominal, 4.2 V fully charged), unprotected, flat or button top. Protected cells are usually too long for the holders, and the pack board provides the protection. Do not use LiFePO4 (3.2 V) cells; the board would over-charge them.
  • Number: two cells for the DUAL pack (2S1P), four for the QUAD (2S2P).
  • Matched cells: every cell must be the same make, model, capacity and age, charged to the same voltage (within 0.1 V) before fitting.
  • Discharge rating: at least 5 A continuous per cell for the DUAL, or at least 3 A per cell for the QUAD, for the full 5 A output. Check that this is the continuous rating, not the peak. Lower-rated cells still work but limit the DUAL's output: 2.6 A cells give about 2.7 A at 5 V, enough for a Pi 5 without power-hungry USB devices. For USB drives or an SSD, use the QUAD pack. Recommended cell: Samsung INR18650-25R or 25RM (2,500 mAh, 20 A continuous).
  • Other packs: any 2S lithium-ion pack (8.4 V full) with a built-in protection circuit and an XT30 plug wired + to +. Set the pack type in the software (see Raspberry Pi configuration) so the charge current suits it.

Pack configurations

Adding cells in parallel increases runtime and shares the load current between cells. At the full 5 A output the pack supplies up to about 4.7 A, so the DUAL pack needs high-drain cells.

Pack Example cells Capacity Usable energy (8.2 V charge) Current per cell at 5 A output Runtime at 6 W (Pi 5, typical) Runtime at 15 W (heavy load) Charge current and time DUAL (2S1P) 2 × 18650, 3,000 mAh 3.0 Ah about 19.5 Wh 4.7 A (use cells rated 10 A or more) about 2.7 h about 1.1 h 1.5 A, about 2.5 h QUAD (2S2P) 4 × 18650, 3,000 mAh 6.0 Ah about 39 Wh 2.4 A about 5.5 h about 2.2 h 2.0 A, about 3.5 h

Usable energy assumes the software's 8.2 V charge voltage, which stores about 10 % less than charging to 8.4 V but roughly doubles cell life. Runtimes assume 85 % conversion efficiency and end at the 5 % shutdown point. The software charges at 1.5 A for 2S1P and 2.0 A for 2S2P; set your pack type with UPS_HAT_CELLS_PARALLEL (see Raspberry Pi configuration).

Runtime. Runtime depends on pack capacity and the Pi's load. As a guide, divide the pack energy by the load power and allow about 85 % for conversion losses:

Runtime (h) ≈ 7.2 V × capacity (Ah) × 0.85 ÷ Pi load (W)

For example, a 3,000 mAh pack (21.6 Wh) running a Raspberry Pi 5 that draws 6 W lasts about 2.7 hours when charged to 8.2 V. The software shuts the Pi down before the pack is fully discharged, so the usable runtime is slightly shorter.

docs.text:
Power flows in one direction: USB-C input → charger → system rail (shared with the battery) → 5.1 V converter → back-feed blocker → Pi header. When USB-C power is removed, the battery feeds the system rail instead, with no gap in the output.

Top view of the Rev D board (Ver 1.4), rendered from the production Gerber files. The 40-pin header J2 is fitted underneath; only its pins show on top. The battery protection is on the UPS Pack board, not on the HAT.

J3 Battery connector (XT30, male) Takes the pack's XT30 plug: pad 1 GND (−), pad 2 battery +. SW1 Power button (marked QON) Short press: wakes the board from its off (ship) state. Long press (about 15 s): resets power to the Pi. D2 Green LED (marked CHG) On: charging. Off: charge complete or no input. Blinking: charge fault. D3 Green LED (marked PWR) On: 5.1 V output to the Pi is active. VBUS, PMID, SYS, BAT, 5V1, GND, EE_WP Test pads For service measurements, each marked with its signal: USB-C input, charger input, system rail, battery, 5.1 V output, ground and EEPROM write-protect.

The XT30 plug fits only one way round. It enters from above; to unplug, pull on the plug, not the lead.

Key components

Function Part Role USB-C PD controller ST STUSB4500 Negotiates 5 V, 9 V or 15 V from the adapter. Battery charger and monitor TI BQ25798 Charges the cells, switches between input and battery, measures voltages and currents, and provides the off (ship) mode. Ship switch MOSFET Q6 Disconnects the battery from the HAT in ship mode, under the charger's control. 5.1 V converter TI TPS54620 Steps the system voltage down to a regulated 5.1 V at up to 5 A. Back-feed blocker Diodes AP74700 with MOSFET Stops current flowing back into the board from the Pi's own USB-C supply. PD controller supply BAT54S diode Powers the PD controller from the 5 V rail, so its I²C pins never hold the Pi's bus low, even when the board is off and the Pi runs from its own supply. Battery protector (pack board) HYCON HY2120 with two MOSFETs Watches each cell and disconnects the pack on over-charge, over-discharge or over-current. Two small MOSFETs (2N7002) override it when the switch or the temperature cut-off turns the pack off. Cell balancers (pack board) HYCON HY2213, one per cell Bleeds a cell above 4.20 V so the cells stay matched. Temperature cut-off (pack board) LM393 comparator with NTC sensors Switches the pack off above about 60 °C. docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
The board is designed for the Raspberry Pi 5 and works with any Raspberry Pi that has the standard 40-pin header.

Raspberry Pi model Supported Notes Raspberry Pi 5 (all memory sizes) Yes, fully Full 5 A output. HAT+ ID read automatically. Raspberry Pi 4 Model B Yes Power and battery monitoring work. The HAT+ ID may not be read by older firmware; this does not affect operation. Raspberry Pi 3 Model B / B+ Yes As for Pi 4. Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W / Zero W Electrically yes The board is larger than a Zero and overhangs it. Raspberry Pi 400 / 500, Compute Modules No No standard 40-pin HAT header.

Operating system: Raspberry Pi OS (Bookworm or later) is recommended. Any Linux with I²C support and Python 3 can run the monitoring software.

Other HATs: the board uses only header pins 3 and 5 (I²C1) and GPIO24 (EEPROM write-protect). Other HATs that use I²C1 can share the bus, as long as they do not use addresses 0x28 or 0x6B.

Cases and coolers: the Raspberry Pi Active Cooler and most low-profile heatsinks fit underneath when the board is mounted on standoffs tall enough to clear them. Check the clearance before tightening the screws.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You will need four M2.5 standoffs with screws, a USB-C PD adapter that offers 9 V or 15 V at 3 A, and the UPS Pack board with its cells (see Battery requirements).

  1. Shut down the Raspberry Pi and unplug all power, including its own USB-C supply.
  2. If you use the Active Cooler or a heatsink, fit it to the Pi first.
  3. Screw the four M2.5 standoffs to the Pi's mounting holes.
  4. Line up the board's 40-pin header with the Pi's GPIO pins and press it down evenly until it sits on the standoffs. Check that no pins are offset by one row or column.
  5. Fix the board to the standoffs with the four screws.
  6. Prepare the pack. With its switch OFF, measure each cell and keep them within 0.1 V of each other. Fit the cells following the + marks: BT1 (and BT3) first, then BT2 (and BT4).
  7. Switch the pack ON and plug its XT30 lead into J3.
  8. Connect the USB-C adapter to J1. The PWR LED lights, the Pi starts, and the CHG LED lights while the cells charge. A newly fitted pack gives no output until the HAT has had USB-C power once, so the first start must be on the adapter.
  9. Continue with Raspberry Pi configuration.

Do not connect a power supply to the Pi's own USB-C port; the board supplies everything the Pi needs. If one is connected by mistake, the board's back-feed blocker stops it driving current into the board.

To start the board from battery alone (no adapter), press SW1 briefly.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• 5.1 V, 5 A output to the Pi through the GPIO header, enough for a Raspberry Pi 5 under full load.
  • USB-C Power Delivery input. Negotiates 5 V, 9 V or 15 V at up to 3 A (45 W) from a USB-C PD adapter, so the board can run the Pi and charge the battery at the same time.
  • Seamless switchover. When input power is removed, the battery takes over with no interruption to the Pi.
  • Plug-in battery pack. The UPS Pack board holds two 18650 cells (DUAL, 2S1P) or four (QUAD, 2S2P) and plugs into the HAT's XT30 connector. Any 2S lithium-ion pack with its own protection and an XT30 plug also works.
  • Battery protection on the pack board, right at the cells:
  • Per-cell over-charge protection at 4.25 V and over-discharge protection at 2.80 V.
  • Over-current and short-circuit cut-off (about 8 A or more, sensed across the protection MOSFETs) and a 10 A fuse.
  • Temperature cut-off: the pack switches itself off above about 60 °C and back on below about 56 °C.
  • Automatic balancing: a cell above 4.20 V is bled down, so the cells stay matched.
  • An on/off switch for storage and transport.
  • Long-life charging to 8.2 V (4.1 V per cell) once the software is installed, for roughly twice the cell life of charging to 4.2 V per cell. Charger safety timer and temperature regulation are built in.
  • Low-battery cut-off on the HAT at about 2.8 V per cell, so the cells are not deeply discharged even if the Pi's software is not running.
  • Ship mode. After a shutdown on battery, the HAT disconnects the battery and draws only microamps.
  • Output current limit of about 7–10 A in the HAT's 5.1 V converter, behind the pack's own over-current protection and fuse.
  • Not provided: a cold-charging limit. The pack cuts off when hot, but nothing stops charging below 0 °C, so keep the cells within the limits in the safety section.
  • Battery monitoring over I²C. Battery voltage, battery current (charge and discharge), input voltage and current, system voltage and charger status can all be read from the Pi.
  • Safe shutdown. The ups-hat software on the Pi shuts it down at 5 % remaining charge, then switches the board fully off to protect the battery. It installs from GitHub with pip.
  • Back-feed protection. The board's output cannot be driven backwards if a supply is also plugged into the Pi's own USB-C port.
  • On-board HAT+ ID EEPROM, so the Pi identifies the board and loads its settings automatically.

docs.title: Operation
docs.text:
The board has no on-board processor. The Raspberry Pi reads the board over I²C and decides when to shut down, so the ups-hat service must be installed for safe shutdowns (see Raspberry Pi configuration).

State What happens LEDs Mains power Adapter powers the Pi and charges the battery. PWR on; CHG on while charging Battery power Battery powers the Pi with no interruption. PWR on; CHG off Low battery The ups-hat service shuts the Pi down at 5 % remaining. PWR on until shutdown completes Off (ship mode) After a shutdown on battery, the board disconnects the battery. Standby drain is a few microamps. All off Hardware cut-off If no software acts, the output switches off at about 5.6 V pack voltage. PWR off

Turning on: plug in the USB-C adapter, or press SW1 briefly to start from battery.

Turning off: shut down the Pi normally (sudo poweroff). On battery, the shutdown hook then switches the board off. On mains, the board stays powered and the Pi halts; unplug the adapter or restart the Pi with its power button.

After a power cut: when the adapter is reconnected, the board wakes and the Pi starts automatically, even if the battery was flat.

Pack switch and temperature cut-off. The pack's own switch turns its output off completely; use it for storage and transport. If the cells reach about 60 °C, the pack switches itself off. On the HAT, after the switch is turned back ON or the cells have cooled below about 56 °C, the pack stays off until the HAT next has USB-C power: connect the adapter to bring it back. Without an adapter connected, the Pi then loses power without a clean shutdown, so give the pack ventilation and keep it out of the sun.

Temperature limits. Keep the board, the pack and the Pi within these limits:

Condition Min Max Notes Running, on the adapter or on battery 0 °C 45 °C Air around the board and the pack. The Raspberry Pi 5 itself is rated to 50 °C Charging the cells 0 °C 45 °C Nothing on the board or the pack stops charging outside this range Cells, at any time — 60 °C The pack switches itself off at about 60 °C and back on below about 56 °C Storage, board only −20 °C 60 °C In its anti-static bag Storage, cells, under a month −20 °C 45 °C For long-term storage keep them at 10–25 °C

Hot cars. On a hot day the cabin of a parked car can reach 60–75 °C, beyond every limit above. Do not leave the pack in a parked car in summer. If it gets that hot, the pack switches itself off. A Pi powered from the car keeps running from the adapter, but it has no battery backup until the pack cools.

Cold. Frosts below 0 °C occur in inland and alpine Australia. Do not charge the pack below 0 °C: charging a cold lithium cell plates lithium inside it, which permanently reduces its capacity and can cause an internal short. Let a cold pack warm to room temperature before connecting the adapter.

Shutdown hook. The shutdown hook (installed in Raspberry Pi configuration) runs at the very end of every power-off. If no adapter is connected, it puts the charger into ship mode, which switches the board off immediately. If the adapter is connected and the shutdown was for low battery, it power-cycles the Pi so that it boots on mains. It does nothing on a reboot, or after a normal shutdown on mains.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi configuration
docs.text:
These steps assume Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm or later. Run the commands in a terminal on the Pi.

  1. Enable I²C. Run sudo raspi-config and choose Interface Options → I2C, or add this line to /boot/firmware/config.txt:

    dtparam=i2c_arm=on

  2. Download the software and install the ups_hat library. This also installs the ups-hat command.

    sudo apt install -y git python3-pip
git clone https://github.com/PinGoblin/UPS_HAT
cd UPS_HAT
sudo pip install --break-system-packages .

  3. Install the ups-hat service and its shutdown hook. The service watches the battery and shuts the Pi down when it runs low. The hook switches the board off at the end of a power-off on battery.

    sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/ups-hat
sudo cp -r examples /usr/local/lib/ups-hat/
sudo cp examples/systemd/ups-hat.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo cp examples/systemd/ups-hat-shutdown /usr/lib/systemd/system-shutdown/
sudo chmod +x /usr/lib/systemd/system-shutdown/ups-hat-shutdown

  4. Tell the software your pack type. Open the service file with sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/ups-hat.service and set these lines:

    Environment=UPS_HAT_CELLS_PARALLEL=1
Environment=UPS_HAT_CELL_MAH=3000

    UPS_HAT_CELLS_PARALLEL is 1 for the DUAL pack (2S1P, charged at 1.5 A) and 2 for the QUAD pack or a larger third-party pack (2S2P, charged at 2.0 A). UPS_HAT_CELL_MAH is the capacity of one cell. Then start the service:

    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now ups-hat

  5. Raspberry Pi 5 only: allow full USB current. The Pi 5 may not detect a 5 A supply through the GPIO header, so by default it limits USB peripherals to 600 mA and may show a low-power warning. Add this line to /boot/firmware/config.txt:

    usb_max_current_enable=1

    Then run sudo rpi-eeprom-config --edit and add this line:

    PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000

  6. Reboot with sudo reboot.

  7. Check the board and the software. i2cdetect -y 1 should list 28 and 6b, ups-hat status should print a report with no critical faults, and systemctl status ups-hat should show the service as active. If not, see Troubleshooting.

The UPS HAT+ API section has more detail on the library, the service and the shutdown hook, and on using the board from MicroPython boards.

docs.title: Power sources
docs.text:
The USB-C adapter must support USB Power Delivery (PD) at 9 V or 15 V, 3 A (27 W or more). A 15 V, 3 A (45 W) adapter is needed to run the Pi at its full 5 A and charge the pack at the same time. The Pi's 5.1 V supply is the same from every source; the source only sets how much power the Pi can draw.

On the adapter. Power the adapter cannot cover is drawn from the pack, if it is connected and charged.

Above 22 W the pack makes up the difference and slowly discharges 5 V, 3 A (PD or USB-C 3 A) 2.8 ≈ 11 ≈ 2.2 Not supported. The Pi runs from the pack until it is flat

With the pack flat, switched off or tripped, nothing makes up a shortfall: if the Pi draws more than the adapter's figure, the 5.1 V output switches off. The software warns when the adapter offers less than 9 V, or when the pack is discharging on mains.

On battery. With no adapter, the Pi has the full 25.5 W (5 A) at every pack voltage down to the software shutdown. Pack current rises as the pack voltage falls.

At a typical 8 W Pi 5 load the pack supplies about 1.1–1.5 A. Every figure stays below the pack's overcurrent trip (about 8 A at the lowest); cells must be rated for at least 5 A continuous.

Figures are calculated, not yet measured. They assume about 93–95 % charger efficiency and about 92 % from the system rail to the Pi header.

docs.title: Important safety information
docs.text:
Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy. Misuse can cause fire, burns or explosion. Read and follow these instructions.

Battery

  • Use only new, unprotected 18650 lithium-ion cells from a reputable manufacturer, rated for at least 5 A continuous discharge (higher-rated cells run cooler and last longer). Never use cells that are swollen, dented, leaking or hot, or that have a torn or damaged wrap.
  • Every cell must be the same make, model, capacity and age. Charge them to the same voltage (within 0.1 V) before fitting. On the QUAD pack the paired cells are joined directly, so two cells at different voltages pass a large current between them the moment they are fitted.
  • Fit cells only with the pack's switch OFF, following the + marks in each holder. Half the holders face the other way.
  • Other packs: use only 2S lithium-ion packs that have their own protection circuit (BMS), with an XT30 plug wired to the standard (+ to the contact marked +). The HAT has no reverse-polarity protection, and a pack wired backwards will damage it.
  • The board cannot measure battery temperature. The pack switches itself off above about 60 °C, but nothing stops charging in the cold: charge only between 0 °C and 45 °C, and keep the cells away from direct sunlight and from heat sources, including the board itself.
  • Do not short the cell terminals, the pack's test pads or the XT30 contacts.
  • Do not leave a charging battery near flammable materials.

Board

  • Disconnect the battery and USB-C power before fitting or removing the board, or touching anything on the Pi's header.
  • The inductors and power ICs become hot to the touch at full 5 A load. Do not touch them while operating, and allow airflow around the board.
  • Do not operate the board in an enclosure without ventilation, near water, or in condensing humidity.
  • Use a USB-C power adapter from a reputable manufacturer, certified to your country's safety standards.
  • Handle the board by its edges and use anti-static precautions. Electrostatic discharge can damage the components.
  • Do not modify the boards or replace the pack's fuse with a higher rating.

Intended use: this is a power accessory for a Raspberry Pi in indoor, non-critical applications. Do not use it in medical, life-support or safety-critical equipment.

If the board or battery smells of burning, smokes, or becomes unusually hot, disconnect USB-C power, then disconnect the battery if it is safe to do so, and move away from it.

docs.title: Shipping, storage and disposal
docs.text:
As supplied: the board ships without a battery in an anti-static bag. It contains no lithium cells, so it is not classed as dangerous goods and can be sent by standard post or air freight.

Shipping a unit with a battery fitted (for example, returning a complete system): lithium-ion batteries are regulated dangerous goods (UN3480 for batteries alone, UN3481 when packed with or fitted in equipment).

  • Remove the cells from their holders before packing, and pack them separately in individual insulating sleeves or cases.
  • For air transport, discharge the battery to 30 % charge or less.
  • Pack the battery so it cannot move, be crushed or short-circuit.
  • Check your carrier's rules before sending. Many postal services accept only batteries fitted in equipment, or ban them from air mail entirely.

Storage

  • Store the boards in their anti-static bags in a dry place between −20 °C and 60 °C.
  • For storage longer than a week, shut down the Pi on battery so the HAT enters ship mode, then switch the pack OFF. Switched on, the pack's temperature monitor draws about 0.5 mA (about 12 mAh a day). Unplugged from the HAT, a pack switched OFF still draws about 0.25 mA (about 6 mAh a day).
  • For storage longer than a month, charge the battery to about 50 % first, or remove the cells.
  • Store batteries between 10 °C and 25 °C, away from flammable materials, and check their charge every 3 months.

Disposal: do not put the board or battery in household waste. Take electronic waste and lithium batteries to an approved recycling point. Tape over the battery terminals before recycling.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
The ups_hat library and its ups-hat service do everything the board needs from the Pi. They install from GitHub with pip (see Raspberry Pi configuration). The UPS HAT+ API section documents the library in full.

What it does

  • Reads the charger every 2 seconds: battery voltage and current, input voltage and current, system voltage and charger status.
  • Sets up the charger at start-up: watchdog off, charge voltage 8.2 V, charge current for your pack type, and an input current limit that matches the USB-C adapter.
  • Tracks remaining charge by counting the current into and out of the battery, re-calibrated at every full charge.
  • Reports faults, with advice, to the system journal (see Fault codes).
  • Shuts the Pi down on battery power at 5 % remaining, or sooner if the battery voltage under load falls to 6.2 V.
  • Switches the board fully off (ship mode) at the end of a power-off on battery.

Commands

Command What it does ups-hat status Prints a one-off report: readings, charge, adapter and faults. ups-hat watch Live report, refreshed every 2 seconds. ups-hat faults Lists every fault code and what to do about it. systemctl status ups-hat Shows whether the service is running. journalctl -u ups-hat -f Shows live readings and events. sudo systemctl restart ups-hat Applies changes to the pack type in /etc/systemd/system/ups-hat.service (run sudo systemctl daemon-reload first). cd UPS_HAT && git pull && sudo pip install --break-system-packages . Installs a software update, then sudo systemctl restart ups-hat. sudo systemctl disable --now ups-hat then sudo pip uninstall --break-system-packages ups-hat Removes the software. Also delete the service file and the shutdown hook.

Settings stay in the charger. With the watchdog off, the charger keeps the software's settings even if the service stops. It returns to its hardware defaults (8.4 V, 1 A) only when the cells are disconnected, until the service runs again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Likely cause What to do Nothing happens when the pack is plugged in Pack switch OFF; a newly fitted pack, or a pack just switched back ON, that has not yet seen USB-C power; pack below the 6.36 V turn-on; or the pack's protection has switched it off after a deep discharge Switch the pack ON. Plug in the USB-C adapter: it wakes the board and the pack, and charges the pack. After a ship-mode shutdown, press SW1. Board runs from the adapter but never from the battery Pack switched off, a cell missing or reversed, pack over-discharged, or the pack's temperature cut-off is active Unplug the adapter and the pack. Check the pack switch and each cell's orientation. Let a hot pack cool, then reconnect and charge for at least 30 minutes. PWR LED off on battery, but on with the adapter Cells are flat, or the pack's over-discharge protection has switched it off Charge with the adapter connected for at least 30 minutes. If it still will not run on battery, measure each cell; replace any cell below 2.0 V. Battery will not charge at all A cell is above 4.25 V, so the pack blocks charging; or a cell is dead Measure each cell. Replace a dead or mismatched cell with a new cell matching the other. Pack switches off by itself Temperature cut-off (about 60 °C) Let it cool, then connect the adapter to bring it back. Improve ventilation round the pack, keep it out of the sun and away from the board's hot parts. CHG LED blinking, battery not charging Charge fault, such as the charge safety timer expiring or a cell over-voltage Unplug and reconnect the adapter. If it continues, check each cell's voltage and replace mismatched cells. i2cdetect -y 1 does not show 6b or 28 I²C not enabled, or the board is not seated correctly Enable I²C with sudo raspi-config and reboot. Check the header is not offset by a pin. ups-hat log shows No such file or directory: /dev/i2c-1 I²C is not enabled Enable I²C with sudo raspi-config and reboot. ups-hat log shows Remote I/O error The board was off, or another device is holding the bus Check the PWR LED is on. Remove other I²C HATs and try again. Battery current reads 0 A, or no readings The ups-hat service is not running Start it with sudo systemctl enable --now ups-hat, or install it (see Raspberry Pi configuration). Charging at 8.4 V or 1 A after unplugging the pack Disconnecting the pack resets the charger to its defaults Normal. The service re-applies its settings within a few seconds. Charge % wrong after fitting new cells The estimate re-calibrates at the next full charge Charge fully once with the adapter connected, and check that UPS_HAT_CELLS_PARALLEL and UPS_HAT_CELL_MAH in the service match your pack. Runtime much shorter than expected Cells are mismatched or worn, so the weaker cell reaches its cut-off first Replace all cells together with new matched cells. Pi 5 shows a low-power or USB current warning The Pi cannot detect a 5 A supply through the header Add usb_max_current_enable=1 and PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000 (see Raspberry Pi configuration). Pi reboots or freezes under heavy load on battery Cells nearly empty or not rated for the load current Charge the cells. Use cells with a higher discharge rating, or move to the QUAD pack. Charging is slow, or the battery drains while on mains Adapter is 5 V only or under 27 W Use a USB-C PD adapter of 27 W or more with 9 V or 15 V output. Board stays on after sudo poweroff The adapter is connected (by design), or the shutdown hook is not installed On mains, unplug the adapter. Otherwise install the shutdown hook (see Raspberry Pi configuration). Pi does not restart when mains returns The Pi halted on mains and is waiting for its power button Press the Pi's power button, or disconnect and reconnect the adapter.

If the problem continues, note the board's revision and the output of i2cdetect -y 1 and of journalctl -u ups-hat -n 50 before contacting support.
